VALUE OF THE BOOK
Pat Gunkel

About + of what I wrote on the brain has been typed. The other 4
is in notes and for the most part reauires no rewriting but simply
has not been typed, representing ideas not contained in that already
typed (save for development), distinct methods of presentation,
perhaps something of the inseperable 'case' for the foregoing, and
arbitrarily absent from the typescript. These would add to something
over 1,000 pages of single-spaced typing. The book is called
Brain Hypotheses and Their Broader Implications, but the part of
the book representing the second half of the title, the implications,
has never been written, although a large part of it is implicit in
the hard hypotheses and exists in my head or, in nutshells, in that
of the book written. Because the book or body of work is so unusual,
and because I have not pushed the book with any publisher nor submitted
any part nor distillation to a journal, it has sofar gone unobserved
and unused by the scientific community. I suspect this is @ real
tragedy based on my own expectation of the book's importance, I would
like, were it possible, to remedy the situation. Toward this, I list
the various values of the book as I see them, mostly without assigning
them any relative or absolute importance or making their individual
cases. I merely want, in one way, to introduce the reader to the book.

1. Mostly absent in the typescript is a list of all the terms in
neuroscience I encountered and recorded as the first step in making

an exhaustive dictionary of the subject which no one has sofar done,
even though one of the most important things in @ science is that its
terms and concepts be gathered together, defined, and systematized.

2. Basically the inception and foundation of a theoretical neuroscience
including ia a systematization of past ideas, an effort at their
synthesis, a setting forth of preliminary ideas, @ consideration and
establishment of goals, means, problems, directions, orders, &c, @
definition and delimitation of the field, @ treatment of premises,

a treatment of standards, a criticism of present progress, the
seperation of theories and hypotheses, a discussion of frameworks

of relevant experiments, a presentation of working theories, @ recasting
of vocabulary, a schedule for accomplishments, &/or the like.

3-e Argument and evidence for attention to an Benost oh ogy, ie serious
and systematic dual treatment of our ignorance about brain and mind.
Specifically, measures of our ignorance in various fields and matters.
4A, Criticism of the authority, relevance, importance, suppositions,
perfection, completeness, style, methodology, implications, understanding
independence, authenticity, theory, vitality, certainty, generality,

&e of past, present, and future work. Suggested corrections. and
provisions.

5. Exhibition of the exemplary and particular real complexity of
subjects, ideas, things, &c; presentation of typical spectra of ideas
and, from these, of the dimensions, dimensionality, and structure of
ideas generally. One reason for and effect of this is to impugn much
of the manner and matter of current research, which is apparently given
to immense, fatal, unrealized, and unanalyzed oversimplifications.
Argument that this inherent complexity speciously or innocuously faults
many negative, bothersome, and mysterious finds, First recognition,
presentation, and analysis of the most important spectra, Argument
that in real nervous systems these distinctions and mechanisms may
coexist and possibly, but only possibly, cooperate.

: <
6. Show something, and by attempt all, of the structure of neuroscience,\
eg by setting forth the interconnexion of concepts, the ideal and actual
branching of spectra of ideas, the overall rivers of possibility.

7. Purposes of neuroscience and their importances are given and
distinguished from those of the past.

8. Attempts are made to blueprint the manufacturing of mechanical
beings: what we should do, what we must know, what class of minds can
exist that do not exist in nature, how natural minds could be extended,
what can be done now, why must it be done, &c.

9. A program for determining what makes m@n more than animals is given
and & comprehensive description of possible and probable neuroevolutionar,
changes is begun.

10. Methods for the simultaneous and usable presentation and effective
condensation of present knowledge are given, including the beginnings

of an exhaustive neurographic atlas.

il. Innumerable novel concepts of the neurology of emotion, thought,
memory, @ction, purpose, development, perception, &c are created.

12. There is an attempt to develop simultaneously ideas that are
superficially or in fact contradictory.

13. Many old and new ideas of the design and function of the cerebellun,
hippocampus, cerebrocortex, basal ganglia, reticular formation, brainstem
general structures, cell column, cells, &c are simultaneously set forth
and compared.

14. Re #11, attempts to give 'adequate' and ‘comprehensive! treatments
of these are made.

15. The order of the world is treated as an important subject in itself,
hitherto neglected.

16. Computers and brains are distinguished.

17. The dimensions of the electrophysiology of lone neurons are defined.
18. An attempt is made to exhaust the typology and structure of neurons.
19. Some of the broad, philosophic consequences of my ideas are given.
20. Various new and important experiments are suggested.

el. Some nonmathematical theory of electroencephalography is given.

22. New theories of human psychology and epistemology are given.

23. There is @ massive analysis of possible bases for vision.

24, The book causes one to think persistently and deeply about the
theoretical side of neuroscientific data. It is intended to trigger
the sudden growth of world theoretical neuroscience. It is intended

to 'seed* neuroscience with a plethora of ideas that these be developed
by others and tested in their work. It is intended to cause
neuroscientists to look at all sides of matters in @ 'topological'
fashion, It is intended to improve the originality of neuroscience.

It is intended to begin at this time the formulation of comprehensive
theories of nervous systems and minds. It is intended to cause
neuroscience to assume @ new importance. It has many other purposes.

CQVMENT ON THE THEORY BEHIND THE WRITING OF THIS BOOK
Pat Gunkel

This book obviously displays considerable density, obscurity, and novelty
of language and thought. Everyone objects to this and supposes it a "mistake",
Everyone, thet is, but myself. I intentionally chose, in this book and in my
life, to spend all my energy on exact, true, progressive, and beautiful thinking
and my own intuition of what I would be doing. I believed that I should try to
maximize my control over effect. These things because in everyone's life and
in society's there are moments, such as James Joyce's “epiphanies", of
transcendent enlightenment so important that despite their fewness or even
uniquity they are equal to or greater than all the signifigance, clarity, and
labor of the intervening or preceding intervals, the conventional styles and
ideas, the conventional notions about human eapacity, and all or an infinity
of triviality; and there are standards; and in today's society and all of history
one sees the problem that standards are lowered, standards of exertion, belief,
& to arbitrary or infinitesimal points, whereas, taking "exertion" as the
example, exertion leads to later ease, memorization aids memorization and is
the basis of subsequent thought, & so that how much better and temporarily
infinite it would be if everyone aggraded standards to bootstrap themselves
to true optimal standards; so that I decided to raise standards; and I realized
that, properly done, writing and thought intense in the seeming flaws listed
above, could occasionally or abstractly break through and be seen with such
strength of emotion and deciding confidence that all its opacity, density, and
oddity would vanish into a strong cognizance of what was meant and a warm and
justified appreciation.

My ideas and wording combine. These combinations, seen and attended to,
drastically and finally simplify what is before you, what is spun out of them
and these combinations are the basic prejudices of all previous writing and
thought by other men, the important general things, to whose revolutionary
address I put this book, to tear the skirt from off these things and to open
the skies of all possibilities, not secreted and dumb fractions lying pointlessly
here and there upon a field of cowdung. The power of these combinations is

either the power of combination by which the brain's description or anticipatory
intereumbent alternatives.

INTRODUCTION
Pat Gunkel

This is an extremely strange book and it faces an uphill battle in getting
read, accepted, and understood. It may seem otherwise to some, but the truth
is that I did not consciously try to make it difficult, on the contrary, but
I did follow the policy of being indifferent to the difficulties of communi=
cation and at least conventional aestheties as I thought and wrote the thing,
So that my thought would be as mercurial (free, reaching, instantaneous,
isoporic, &¢) as possible. In fact this is more of a problem than appears at
first sight for much of the book and generally "the best ideas? operating at
a certain level of abstraction (and empirical connexion) must necessarily in
writing, and extremely a fortiori in my case, go unrecorded: by far the most
and best part of this book are lost thoughts and completely unavailable to the
reader who is and was not myself. This is something of what is meant by the
intuitive type. Often inspirations mst later, if ever, be laboriously
justified. There are many of the peculiarities of this book for which I feel
there need be no justification, although they may certainly be unconventional.
Rg the poet is a thinker whose mysterious and highly abstract insighta certainly
have no need of annotation, but who can arrive, sometimes specifically by the
use of incanmunicative means (which however are beautiful and thus “artistic”
manifestations) such as metaphorie steppingstones that float in space or as
Smoky metaphors thaiincomprehensibiy formed, complex, and turned and yet
convey (again perhaps secondarily) incomparable delight; if the dominant
theories of this book are correct, such subtleties of ghostlike thought are
man in his highest and true type, the agency behind the grosser works that
settle as the deceptive dregs of untraceable, unimaginably subtle, heavenward
thought. It is enough that we can have the fruits of such thought and the
larger patterns that drift away from it, to be followed only by thought of
identical kind, rather than to mimie (per tradition) the gross, preposterous,
and feeble irrelevances that remain. The death of the spirit of man and of
science (in its essential form) are what is seen when ghostly thought is
thrown aside'as vague.

This book is an altar to that thought.

The poet in history was often an adviser to kings, and to whom does one
go to understand the meaning of life but the poet? The poet is concerned
with the flight of things and the image of the world is alate. It is the
expanse, complexity, and specificity of the world that is the source, the
reference, and the terminus of ideas or the real form of things for things
in their meaningful essence are inextractable from experience in its entirety;
yet experience is ever incomplete and the things that fall within this
truncated experience are arrows that point to horizons infinitely distant
that cannot be brought within the present as parts thereof, so that the poet
is merely concerned with the vastest intercomparison of these arrows and
what he utters thereupon cannot be rewritten else it will point elsewhere,
perhaps nowhere, and earn destruction. Who would contain lightning in a glass
case, count the sand upon the shore, or seulpture a river? Ah, many! But
a little girl is her own lesson, too profound and too trivial to be otherwise,

the tides now racing over these things, There are diverse personal purposes in

When I set out to explain the brain I did not foresee what I was getting ine
to beeause the requirements for an explanation have never been defined. So now
that it appears to me I may have succeeded in explaining the brain I encounter
an even greater problem of explaining what I mean. Not only that, "proof" is
also wanted and undefined. Which in turns presupposes “conviction” of any
relevant parties, in short, a mass effect. So my task, and ultimate accomplishment
potentially, is quadrupled. I suppose it might be wise to circulate a questionaire
in connexion with these issues and to stipulate, at its close, that, the criteria
having been met, the brain will have been adQuately "explained". But I fear that
even this discussion will be incendiary and make an explanation more dubious so
I and my burden are actually backsliding. Oh, how hopeless! Let me spare the
questionaire, then, and devise my own criteria with an invitation to the rambunctious
reader to exercise his wits on them, demanding proof of prooflessness and defense
of criticism, with the stipulation that in the end the reader will have regressed
for want of definition of these concepts.

It is necessary, or at least desirable, that:

i. The style be impeccably and unsuspectably academic: florid, familiar, stiff,
circular, illogical, offensive, limit self-disguising, pretentious and yet
self-denying, heavy, incomprehens iblé""Stmiess, trivial in data and message, old,
sensational, authoritative, indirect, work-extending, complimentary, designing,
orthographic, illustrative, confused, successional, soporific, amnesic, funded,
conservative, haphazardly formal, underwritten by a fad, pessimistic, insulting,
and full of shibboleths. Why? Only God knows.

ii. I mst have performed some experiments, regardless of their novelty or
relevance, and these mist take up most of the presentation with negligibles. These
must heve confirmed the theory but not have proved anything (which would be suspect
as too ambitious), although I mst do my best to disguise them as seemingly proving
it (the paradox never having been “explained"),

iii. I mst “answer” all the problems (many themselves doubtful) and data.

iv. I must make a set of predictions, to add to future controversy, to draw on
the obvious, and to exercise the falsehoods of science. I mst look under the
microscope and see something written there, “Bingot* Which observation mst be
repeated many times by many laboratories under various conditions, so that it can
become the new dogma.

vo Fifty years mst have passed and the explanation have thus become a defense
of now-controversial tradition.

vi. I must have wooed a fanatical following and have exchanged it for everyone
now working in academe, industry, and government and thereby suborned institutional
acceptance.

viie I must have since gotten a spot for myself on TV.

viii. Of course, I must have eliminated all contradictions in my work, and
carefully bury or reface the road over which I have come, not only to prove my
theory but to enhance my genius and future livelihood as a common simplifier.

ix, I mst come upon my discovery by way of a team, sane collaborators, and
a clue.

x. Imust have shot and nailed down all potential and real competitors by any
means availible, including bribery, sarcasm, or machinations to cut off their funds.

xi, Everybody mst believe, too.

This may seem an awful lot, but other people have succeeded in the past, so I
must read books on mass behavior.

THE PROBLEMS IN READING THIS BOOK
Pat Gunkel

The vocabulary 1s END large.
Many words are invented.

Many words are reapplied.

The book lacks organization: as it is, it is nonlinear and improgressive.

The author is wise from his ignorance: others are ignorant of this wisdom.
Theoretic neuroscience is conceived for the first time. There is no readership.
Whole batteries of new concepts are used. The form and content of these is often
extremely novel.
The many concepts form and are initially inseperable fram a great web of processes.
The territory covered is gigantic and the approach necessarily summary and implicit.
The author's mind moves at a very high speed upon equally high trajectories.

Many ideas are pursued at once. These ideas may or may not have something to

do with each other.

The statement is staccato or laborious, peremptory, abstract, contradictory,
abstruse, percussive, kaleidoscopic, pointillist, marching, racy, preposterous,
unsequential, irreprtitive, &= to a surprising degree.

Rare knowledgability is presumed.

The style is irreverent, critical, iconoclastic, apocalyptic, unbelievably dense,
experimental, "hyper-technical", elliptic, metaphoric, associative, dissonant,
and overwhelming. It is the sole nonfiction Finnegans Wake.

Many ideas are reapplied, stretched, and put through a fantastic pallet.
Synthesis of past neuroscience is implicit: there are few compass points for the
consequent reader.

The subtlety, integrity, agility, and power of attention presumed is unique.

The style is morphologic and clusteral.

Ideas are treated in the way of a dynamics instead of statics, whereas the

A VIEW OF THE WORLD CONSEQUENT UPGN MY IDEAS OF THE BRAIN
Pat Gunkel

As originally anticipated, my understandings about likely and possible brain
function are full of signifigance for man’s view of his own world. Some of these
consequences are:

1. Man is untrustworthy in the short and longterm, in the one and the many, and
especially in the present and future possible and probable world due to their
peculiar setting.

2. Man is defective, limited, determined, &.

3. Man is with meaning.

4. Man is inspecific.

5. Ideas are inspecific.

6. Motivations, ideas, perceptions, & are complex and distributed.

7, These things are mysterious.

8. The mystery in the world is indefinitely great, both qualitatively and
quantitatively.

9. Man’s success is due to his self-transcendence. Man's rate thereof is unnecessarily
slow. The dynamic process which is man in his higher meaning is strictly
limited by his static mechanisms,

10, Being is above any individual man, organism, moment of time.

11. ‘The natural processes of the world are far more complex than we might suppose.

12. Understanding and mental health require a large and random view of a large and
random (or naturally formed and adequate) world.

13. Ignorance about our own natures causes much of our trouble as social and individual
beings. This ignorance is unnecessary.

14. The amount of meaning in the world is infinite.

15. "God", a peculiar synthesis of the whole active in the constant organization of
behavior, is natural; it is the point where the whole refers to itself in fullest
self-transcendence, and it is the idea of continuity amid change and of change
amid any continuity.

16, Bizarre unconscious ideas of the world are contimally forming owing to variations
of underlying motivation, self-ignorance, intrusions of unfortunate motivations,
insidious accretions, surprising crystallizations of the entire mind, at the
periphery of conscious processes, &. Peculiar types of behavior are precipite-
ting from these and assuming excessive signifigance.

17. The continual lapsing of the mind into static understandings is turning ephemera,
processes, aspects, and machinery into absolutes, wholes, substances, and
ultimates in a highly destructive and completely misleading fashion. The world
is thus becoming a junkpile of these arbitrary epiphenomena with their arbitrary
motivations.

18. No totally specific complex behaviors are inherited in the prain, tho this may
be in err. Instead there are indefinite, however strong and peculiar, tendencies
that are perhaps similarly worrisome from the standpoint of possible human virtue
and the explanation of society.

19. It should not be overly hard and it is not impossible to intervene in man's
biological constitution for man's radical benefit and to model machines around
the principles derived from a study of the brain wholly doing avay with the
undesirable peculiarities found in man as a reflection of this constitution. It
is easy to design machines zillions of times superior to men as living beings.
These machines should inherit the earth.

20. Man's brain has given the world the possibility of absolute progress and absolute
appreciation.

TH: END GF A STUDY OF THE BRAIN
Pat Gunkel

I am ending my study of the brain and here is whys
The initial advantages I had by entering a field quickly with total ignorance in
the beginning are passing or passed. I have begun to acquire the stickiness of
my own ideas, their presuppositions, and the ideas and data of the field. My
enthusiasm caused by a naive spectacle, and so valuable in seeing things
novelly &, is passing. I now think others can use my ideas better than I. ‘The
‘metaphors and ‘textures' I was able to draw on by my experience of things
outside this field are exhausted, invalid, confusing one another, inactive, &.
Many general or particular problems that originally excited me do so no longer,
eg because I have ‘satisfactorily’ explained them.
The ideas I now have are becaming too numerous and trivial, ironically at the
same time as they may appear more profound or be the more interesting, and are
pressing too strongly against the boundaries of our ignorance, the maniness of
my assumptions, and are drawing too heavily on what little we know or only think
we know (double ignorance). I now have too much facility in combining my ideas
and manipulating data to suggest hypotheses, and hypotheses maybe increasingly
formal.
Griteria for explaining the brain, for testing hypotheses, for using ideas, &
are not available. This is too psychologically futile for me to continue it
forever.
Other interests, intentions, obligations, &¢ are pressing on mee It is my method
to only devote a small period of time to any subject: my best creativity is to
do jumping from field to field.
My ideas may exist in too intuitive a form. I can not take the time or do not
have the ability to document the foundations and evidences for my case and that,
differentially, contributed to it originally. The complexity and difficulty
of expressing these ideas, at least at this time, may be infinitely greater than
that of having explained the brain or a part thereof.
There are too many things I could say on too many subjects—not even in a lifetime
could I say all that there is to be said. Saying all this, in addition, may be
irrelevant. Perhaps only a few men will ever truly understand the brain.
I am pressing up against my own ignorance, inabilities, &. I despgrately feel
the relevance, parallelism, essentiality, &re of mathematics, of which subject
I am totally ignorant.
Many things I could do would apparently be wasted because others would not use,
understand, or appreciate them or, just generally, they would not justify
themselves, Studies of chemistry, pathology, psychophysics, & and the preparation
of a fabulous atlas are cases in point.
It was my intention, often, to just show how things could or might be done or
might be and, having done so, not to extend, complete, perfect &re these things.
I was trying to show the dimensions, detail, variety, possible methods, mental
style, & of the field: the book is extremely implicit,
It appears that the explanation of the detailed or concrete operation of the brain
(which may be exactly what some are explicitly or implicitly looking for) might,
in any cases, be too herculean, infinite, complex, incomprehensible, specific, &e
to justify the exertions and might not, in itself, constitute either a general
explanation of the brain or a proof of anything (eg the specificity might be
ambiguous proportionately to its specificity).
I find it impossible to choose from among my possibilities. Many people demand
such choice. Furthermore, I see that if I make things any more complicated it will
simply compound the problem that no one has cared enough to understand what I have
already said. Requests given me by people to simplify & my book seem ignorant or
guilty of similar errors.

I undertook in this study to find out the extent of our knowledge and ignorance
about the brain. I have seen that we suffer from abysmal ignorance. All we seem
to know are scratches on the surface. Here and there there are hints that we
know more, eg general views of the brain's overall function, but these hints are
illusions. I likewise undertook to see if current knowledge could be better
organized, if important theories could be developed out of it, and if it could be
used to gain satisfactory comprehension of the mind's function on same level of
generality. I found everyone of these latter things to be true. Another objective
was to apply what is known and what I could theorize to the problem of whether we
can now or in the course of a few years of work build a mind equal of our,own, and if
so, how. It is premature to answer this question and to say whether I have achieved
the second part, and I vacillate in my opinion, but I have surprised myself on how
possible these are.

Tot IMPORTANCE OF LOGIC TO THE PREEMINENCE GF MAN'S INTELLIGENCE
Pat Gunkel

Surveying the behavior of all animals one is led to suppose in man there is
sane element of genius not to be found elsewhere and perhaps this element is
of a logical kind. Comparing nervous structure and function in man with that
in animals identifiable changes are suggested that could well account for this
distinct logical activity or proficiency. This enjoins an investigation into
the nature of logic and a suspicion that this is not really appreciated. It
may be suggested that cultural acquisition of language elicits logic but it is
also likely that an innate propensity for logic basically enables the
acquisition and application of language: it is appealing to suppose that
language is the product of a logical creature.

Aspects of logic: perfect and imperfect conjunction and dis junction;
universal necessity, particular necessity, universal contingency, particular
contingency, universal impossibility, particular impossibility; singular v
particular concepts; eduction: conversion, obversion, contraposition,
reciprocation, and inversion; contradiction; divisive v collective concept;
quantification; comprehension v extension; deduction v induction; &. These
aspects, falling strictly under the head of logic, join with aspects of our
language, and their underlying mechanisms, and together give intellectual
capacity. Observe any sentence and you will see that its bases are such
logical operations enabling a peculiar sorting of experiential material. At
once it is clear that the existence and definition, and relative exertion, of
these operations distinguish man from all animals. It cannot be without
Signifigance that there are circuits-~more or less known and postulable~—
enabling such operations. Nor is it hgrd to assume the virtual absence of
these circuits, and hence logical operations, in anything below man.
Furthermore, the developmental operation of these circuits and logical
operations will clearly, even distinctively, transfigure mind, liberate self,
and alter throughout the style and products of the brain, the motivations,
the emotions, the perceptions, the behaviors, and the associative processes
that then become thought. It can be said that man is a logical intelligence.
In the rest of this paper I will describe the nature of logical operations,
the assumable neurological machinery, and the composition of these two in
the genesis and life of a human being. Elsewhere I will extrapolate the three
to the superhuman.

"Arve An Inebriated Man and An Animal
Comparable Intellectually?"

Patrick Gunkel

I wish to suggest in this paper that a drunk and animal are analogous
in intelligence, inasmuch as a ‘congenital’ drunk would never achieve our
intelligence if he were as drunk as an animal is dumb (assuming that this
is pointful).

It is perhaps significant that damage to the dorsomedial nucleus of the
thalamus, for example, produces a kind of drunkenness, and that there is
some indication, however slight, that damage of this kind, if congenital,
would produce idiocy.

Characteristics of these states are: obvious stupidity, amnesia,
silliness, confusion, disorientation, de-concentration (i.e., loss of
concentration), defect of purpose, vulgarity, defect of insight, irreality,
defect of the sense of time, impairment of consciousness, visceral changes,
etc.

Here is what I must report from being--experimentally--drunk: motor
incoordination, slowness of thought, muddleheadedness, retarded
perception, lapsing and restriction of perception, a kind of closing and
shrinking of the world, autocosm (i.e., a self-created microcosm or private
world, or an equivalent subjective state), poorness of memory, difficulty in
thinking systematically, decrease of purpose, childishness, emotional
blunting and crudification, a lack of seriousness or care, overgeneralized
pleasure (i.e., inability to package and direct pleasure, and to postpone
pleasure and things), simplification of perception, greater illusion,
diminished self-control, aprosexia, excessive perceived harmony of things,
a centering on and yet ‘thinning’ of the present (e.g., a ‘loss of the past and
future’), dissociation of behavior, mental inexactitude or blurredness, loss
of curiosity or habituation (shallow curiosity), overconcern with ‘simply
getting on in the world’ (i.e., with orientation, action, reaction, and
coping), conception yielding to perception or mere sensation, overcertainty,
poor perception of self (i.e. de-objectification), glibness, loss of spontaneity
(e.g., in extremis, "stiffness’), etc.

Now these are very interesting properties, if one assumes that they
could be dimensionally (i.e., as dimensions) inverted by changes in
nervous systems leading up to Homo sapiens, so that their opposites could
be extended or maximized by evolution.

Take just one property. As I write, I see a man out in the field opposite
who is patently drunk. He is standing in the wind and his shirt is flapping.
I see through binoculars that his shirt is sharply detailous (Ze., rich in
detail). I know perfectly well that, in his approximate stupor, this
sharpness that I see is wasted on this man. Yet it is my belief that such an
ability to remain aware of sharpness and detail is an essential to the
development of higher ideas in a human mind. That is, it seems to be a
trait of Man that he is able to sustain and control the processes of his mind.

If these are customary processes for the posterior or lower cortices (i.e.,
portions of the cerebral cortex), then higher cortices are able to modulate
(e.g., inhibit, sustain, intensify, pattern, move in time, complicate, direct,
compare with reality or themselves, delete, etc) these lower processes. At
the level of the lower association cortices it might suffice for the higher
cortices to hold ‘in the mind's eye’ the patterns in the lower cortices, so

When you mentioned yesterday the peculiarity of the basal ganglia,
the extreme convergence of its afferents contrasted with the very incomparable
nondivergence of its efferents, I thought at once to mention that I have never
heard of a structure where the physiologic versus anatomic finds on connectivity
were more discrepant, implying, as wetve discussed before, that there is something
very inaccurate about degeneration and staining methods applied to the basal
ganglia, especially certain of its hypothetic connections, eg Striatocortic,
and the recent crop of finds, throwh the application of new neuroanatonic
methods, that the brain's connections are stranger than thought also came to my
mind, for these new methods producing startling results in cases are really sofar
So little used that surely the complete and true architecture of the brain's
connections, while it may preserve certain old positive ideas, may superimpose
a largely or wholly new quantitative and qualitative picture. Now, of course,
I realize this idea is very upsetting and quite speculative, and I wonder if we
cannot contain it a bit in this wy.

The 29 Je 73 Brain Research carries an article on page 1 by A. Nobin,
et al, "Axonal Degeneration and Regeneration of the Bulbospinal Indolamine Neurons
After 5,6-dihydroxytryptamine Treatment", conbinable with recent work showing
regeneration in the septun, hypothalamus, and elsewhere, suggests to me an hypothesis
that neurons extremely high in neurotransmitters (as producers or no; eg monoaminergic
or cholinergic) may have an ability to regenerate their fibers, or a disproportionate
ability obscuring connectivity patterns implied by degeneration methods. There are
obviously many regions of the brain and many of its fibers that would be obscured
in this way. In any case, there would be a steep scaling of different regions and
fibers if this principle of varying vitality holds. This is particularly interesting
because our Imowledge of many of these qualifying regions is especially poor and,
where there is knowledge of any kind, connective asymmetries are familiarly implied;
at the same time as these regions are of extraordinary importance and to a certain
extent can be classed together. I am thinking of the basal forebrain, the anygdala,
the hypothalamus, the hippocampus, other structures, and the basal ganglia. ‘The
basal ganglia are notably high in putative neurotransmitters and other trophic
Substances, and have that ventricular relationship that I have suggested makes a
structure a candidate for neuroendocrine status, sensu lato or in a novel sense.

recall, that experimentation should be based on peradventures or the systematic
exploration of stochastic ranges, is ideally apposite here, and that someone should
look at a range of these chemically peculiar structures and see whether they are not
typically regencrative to a degree impugning their traditional connectivity, and
with basic importance to the understanding of the brain.

is meant an enhanced dependency on one's brains, conceivably further enhanced

of inherited behavior forcing versatility and innovation and possibly some sort
of cultural continuity. Purposeful intraspecific interindividual aggression
selectively multiplying ingenuity. The emergence of personality and sufficient
intelligence that mating expresses judgment and intellectual affinity. Possibly
such organization of the brain that pleasure arises in and depends on mental
fulfilment and cortic solution of problems besetting the subcortex or the cortex.
Early language and tool using specializing the nervous system for interpersonal
communication, and perhaps therewith selection through expansion of particular
populations, through wars, and through what might be called intrigue or a differential
survival of the wittiest conversants and the most abstract insights. Intense
specialization by virtue of the decisive importance of some state, such as
speech, suddenly polarizing other considerations for organization of the nervous

intelligent and intellectually (eg conversationally) entertaining and, this process
repeated for millenja across vast population, a slow continuous average of better
men from better animals might emerge. In terms of reason, creativity, and speech,
it is conceivable that never before had evolution a nervous specialization with

Unfortunately most of these remarks are based on the brains of dolphins
rather than those of the largest whales. (Dolphins are technically whales.)

I suggest that the specific addition of a motor component to the artificial
mind may be necessary and be the secret of the linear and focal properties of
human thought, through the component necessitating address to and solution of
the finite and arrayed problems of the external world. The presence of this
motoceptive component would be the fundamental for the expression of cognitive
possibilities later in life. Gm the other hand, it may be concluded that the
mere supply of a motivational component, somehow tied to the registration of
sonmehow-proper states in the sensory and gnostic sphere, would be adequate in
conducing to the development of acceptable cognitive and self-conscious
features. Going still further, it may be suggested that the sole need of the
Sensory component is to supply the material for the organization and reference
of thought in the presence of a motivational or polar component somehow aware
of the incrementel1 acceptability of the developmental course and final products
of the gnostic camponent (or the aim of these attempts to define the basis of
syntheses of mind).

It is unsure how essential or useful various degrees of motor reactions may
be in furthering the develoyment of mind, but in a minimal sense, one could
take the presumed evoked potential as a binary or intricate abstract motor
reaction serving the above coordination of thought arising from sensation, and
of course there would be many other simple readings that could substitute and
achieve the end. Conversely, it is unsure how essential or useful various
degrees of sensation might be in such genesis, and it can also be hypothesized
that extremely elementary inputs could suffice for the easy development of
mind, its maintenance, or its arbitrary size; but on weaker ground, perhaps,
for it is somewhat difficult to imagine a seperation of this flow of material
from a constitution of mind, so dependent would mental processes seem upon the
redundant and diverse order seemingly limited to such material and its flow.
(Certainly the mechanisms for the development of mind with exiguous afference
and/or efference are inapparent.)

Nevertheless, little conviction resides in the supposition that there is
any necessity for many types of senses, many muscles or effectors, or for
correspondent differentiation internal to these types. Still, the question
remains what final variety may be necessary in mental interaction with the
external or internal world for reasons of material constitution or for reasons
of triggered organization in either brains or artificial minds of all kinds,
eg such variety and quantity may be necessary to engage and direct the
motivational mechanism and the process of (sensorially a9 interventionally directed)
thought.

& hollow-spherical cortex may be the ideal for artificial minds as well,
enabling the steric anyness of segregated and preponderant connections between
cellular components. So may be its convolution, given the unequal importance

Pat Gunkel

A major purpose in writing this book was to found a science of ontology,
a word derived from the Greek root ont- meaning existence, being, life, or
organism, as I understand. J borrowed the philosophic term because
radically the word is so explicit, corresponds so well with what is actually
happening in science and the world, and is vastly superior to narrower
definitions of a science, eg “artificial intelligence” or *artificial mind”,
whose use has been and would be unfortunate in leading to misunderstanding
and deformation of scientific work and thought, eg through erroneous
constriction and misemphasization. Moreover, the history of the race, the
form of the modern world, and the shadows of things to come strongly limn
the critical need for such an explicit and self-serious science. The science
will be both pure and applied, and, in fact, the very nature of the word
ontology bridges the two, eg transtemporally. In the external world, it is
apparent that science, thought, play, reason, emotion, idea, value, immediacy,
eternity“ possibility, probability, necessity, will, fate, individual and
collective, pure and applied, technical and arbitrary or casual, whole and
part, one thing and another, biology and psychology, psychology and philosophy,
opposites in general, cause and effect, the whole of tims, the whole of
everything, é are coming together as the major theme of the age and of human
history or intelligence, It is apparent that the nature and safety of the
world are confused and that the explicit need for description, explanation,
solution, and address of the world’s (often derived) problems with varying
urgency call for the answers of this proposed science. Accordingly and also,
it is evident that the science is not only timely but also imaginable, feasible,
formiable, incipient, absent, catalytic and perfect, applicable, gradable,
and emergent in my and others’ work, as well as perfectible and proportionate.
So the term paradoxically fuses all these things, eg possible and actual being,
subjective and objective being, theoretical and experimental science, science
for its own and for man's sake, individual and universal purpose, and the
division of human interest; a particularly interesting example is the fusion
or confusion of imagination and experience, ideal and real, abstract and concrete,
passive and active, é&c. The motivation for the science is in the conviction of
the superiority of a tertiary position to warring dichotomies in the patterned
behavior of the human race, or many tertiary positions to many false or misguided
dichotomies; the irony of the science lies in its fascination with the dichotomies.
It can be argued that the world is unnaturally complex and the mind of humanity
too analytic nowadays, and that convergence, synthesis, analyticosynthesis, or
universality is due, contingent, or inevitable. Another reason I had for
proclaiming an ontology is to revolutionize, define, correct, and protect the
motives for neuroscience et al in the future, eg liberating neuroscience fran
narrow pathic, pure or applied, institutional, natural, economic, mundane,
traditional, anthropocentric, experimental, & orientations present in the past,
dominant in the present, and possible in the future. It is, furthermore, my
conviction that we now have the ability to define, precise, and quantitate the
nature, goals, prospects, and good of the class of living beings including
ourselves and our inseperable progeny

Cne of the main functions of this book is to raise the art and science of
neural and general speculation and interrogation to another level. The great
hesitancy of scientists—publicly, privately, or mentally--to speculate on
their work and on science as a whole strikes me as contemptible and is no
longer, in an age when the reasons for science are becoming apparent,
acceptable. Scientists are afraid to speculate on their work because they
prefer it stable and would as soon have their results lie in the slow
rendering of the obvious. They are afraid of their ignorance and dislike
complexity. Asking a question, including finding a question to ask, is
initially very difficult, and many scientists have no and have never developed
any ability and skill at asking questionsy-systematicly, penetrantly, profoundly,
comprehensively, flexibly, alternatively, usefully, and so forth; they lack
the style, psychology, and reason to do so--generally speaking there is far
too mch timidity. Generally scientists have a particular education and
organization of thought which is verbal, nonverbal, unimaginative, traditional,
conservative, defensive, one-track, linear, overcontrolled, rigid, oversystematic,
*literal* (%), performative, nonintuitively learned and passed on, institutional

territories, &¢), minimizing, mistenacious, foggy, overformal, and overlax.

organization, & are what is called for, including eg comprehensive multidisciplinary

CAUSES AND EFFECTS OF ASYMMETRY IN THE BRAIN
Pat Gunkel

Since asymmetry is basicly interpreted in man as verbal v nonverbal, the first
question is what purpose asymmetry served in the lives of man's nonlinguistic
ancestors, justifying the eventual introduction of man's marked asymmetry? Of
course, it could be that asymmetry is qualitatively or quantitatively a product
of early man's beginning linguistic history, in other words, a product of the
use of language, or of some level of thought, conceivably derived from language,
profiting from accentuated asymmetry. A simultaneous question is some degree of
measure of asymmetry, absolutely and relatively, and its application to man's
animal ancestors, and the related but interesting matter of just how far back
and in what form, of sameness of side &, asymmetry goes in various animals: has
it a common value to, say, frog®s, with their asymmetric medial habenular nucleus?

In the matter of dominance and specialization of each side in its own direction,
it is worthwhile noting that dominance or specialization of just one side, say
based on left hemispheric extent of Turck's bundle, would lead to contrastive,
compensatory, and negative specialization of the opposite side, which we could
automatically call dominance of a kind, and, furthermore, any such asymmetry of
function, along with attendant specialization, would strongly encourage the nervous
system to restructure that side, within the limits of its abilities, both currents
of change leading to mutual adaptations and the refinement of asymmetry; however,
it may be that this secondary process was not very advanced,

Also bothersome is the putative absence of any intrinsic qualitative difference
in congenital or early unihemispherie or aconmissural men, insofar as one would
want to attribute any special signifigance to asymmetric structure and function;
however, one is inclined to be very careful in assuming that there are on hand
any cases at all in the literature where no interhemispheric interaction in early life
could have occurred and yet intellectual development is perfectly or variously
normal, Moreover, in this connexion, the question of commissural interaction
may be quite seperate from that of functional necessity of bihemispheric operation,
for the two hemispheres may achieve a kind of synergy merely from cancertion or
division of concerns at subcortic, eg diencephalic or stem levels, or in handling
the external enviroment; functional asymmetry is permissible even in these indirect
terms and there is no proof that this is not what the asymmetry is all about. Of
course, such cases might impugn ideas about the bases of specialization and synergy
resting imperturbably on direct nervous communication.

Related to all this is the puzzle why in a minority of human beings chirality
should be mirror-reversed and in the absence of accompanying functional deficit.

An essential doubt is whether we are even justified in presuming that
there is such a concept as “general dominance", As to the origin of any specializae
tion, did this come from extension or retraction on the dominant or nondominant side?
Inasmuch as there is any specialization, has there been analogous intralateral
specialization, perhaps as the very basis of the interlateral phenomena? If we do
succeed in establishing one, some, or major causes and effects of asymmetry, can
we be sure that there are not others, that the phenomenon is not general, that
throughout the brain or at least in some other structures there are increments of
asymmetry quantitatively or qualitatively hidden by the asymmetries that we have
identified, eg as dominant? Would the brain be as successful if both sides
developed the same dominant structures or does our success rest specificly on an
asymmetry and a superior~inferior relationship? How early in life does asymmetry
appear, and taking us from the ancestors presumed to be less asymmetric? Is
asymmetry, of anysort, but one of many incremental ingredients collectively essential
to man's intellectual superiority but individually inessential?

Multifunctionalism. ordinarily it is thought or it is assumed in theories
that structures of the brain must have only one or one main function or
mode of operation, that they do or can have but one; or, if they have more,
that the number mist be very small and unusual, and perhaps exacts a cost F
or that the function mst be very clearly evidenced in the structure or,
particularly, in the differences and Similarities with other structures;
or, if there are many functions » that these must alternate and that they
must be sequentially and purposefully linked; furthermore, there is a habit
of looking for maximally contrasting and certainly dissimilar explanations
of function for different structures 3; there is also a certain tendency to
limit function on the basis of structure or to limit it arbitrarily. The
truth is that there may be, that it may even be the rule, that structures
may have an indefinite number of indepatient, semiindependent, and dependent
functions, and functions paying negligible attention to, at least obvious,
structural peculiarities and differences «.

Multistructuralism. Obversely, functions may be carried out by the integral
or duplicative work of many different structures, wheneas there is often a
tendency of workers to confine in their projections functions to unique and
sole structures, The miltiplicity of possible structural bases in a tissue,
by theory or fact, able to explain assumed functions is just overwhelming,
almost regardless of the functions to which structures would be ascribed;
and this holds for structures both large and tiny in the anatomic hierarchy.
In connexion with both mltistructuralism and multifunctionalism, it is
important to keep in mind that the addition of new structures and funetions
may have a radical bearing on the old, and that this too warrants a valid
theory.

There is a tendency to suppose that an abstract triangle (whatever that may be,
since eg it may be dynamic and complex mental processes expressed to a degree,
even in the best insight a man ever had) is what the mind is occupied with when a
triangular form in the real world is perceived. Yet concrete forms such as
concrete triangles may actually be mch more specialized and even much more
generalized ‘thingst. It is a truism that things are perceived as a function of
setting and position in the stream of consciousness and biases of the observer.

En fact a brain is continually in the midst of subjective perspectives as if it

were specifically these perspectives, and not real or seeming parts, that are the
brain's concern and, for practical purposes, the brain's means for seeing ‘things’.
An example might be a triangle sitting on the ground and confronted by a rabbit.

The typical occurrence of any such form (and it is typical occurrences wherein a
triangle has signifigance) might be with a particular type and proportion of
triangle with its large base down or continuous with the ground or foreground,

and certainly with what only approaches a rigidly and properly geometrie (much
less axiomatic?!) triangle and a 2-dimensional, nonsolid, and perhaps empty triangle
as opposed, say, to a nose or treetop. It may actually be advantageous for an
animal (or a mant) to customarily pereeive a triangle as basedown and without

high, complete, or any rotatory invariance (indeed, the rotated triangle may

more nearly suggest to the animal another form at another orientation). (Same)
rotatory invariance may actually bring unnecessary complexity into the seene or

act. Men have difficulty substituting perspectives, even if the adopted perspective
is arbitrary: reversing optical illusions, reading upside down, reversing thought
processes, re-examining a picture, &. It is possible the very frequency of things
or the complex associative frequency of things determines much of the way we look

at things and gives a certain arbitrariness to perspective (since alternative
associations of things and depths of association are potentially infinite, some
exclusion and some choice mst occur). It may be that animals differ in the length
and complexity of the evoked potential and in the tenacity with which the hippocampus
perpetuates interests, and hence came to differ in their quotient of self-dissatisfac~

A METHOD FOR DIVULGING THE STRUCTURE OF RECOGNITION
Pat Gunkel

One takes a tachistoscope, computer with a cathode ray tube (CRT), or a
movie and uses these to show a series of objects or scenes in variously
randomized sequence, say at a flicker rate or a variously randomly varying
rate, and observes. The things projected may be few in number, such as 2 or
3 scenes, repeated, or all different. The projection may go on for just
5 seconds or all day or for weeks. The set of things shown may or may not
be chosen for types of similarity or for greatest degree or type of
heterogeneity or dissimilarity, Sequence randomization may or may not be
essential, Showing may be adjusted to the subject, say as to rate. Good
projection material would be a set of extremely complicated natural scenes.

One might specially randomize (say intrascenically) for successive location,
orientation, size, distortion, obscuration, complexity, &re. Qne may take
the rate of presentation up to the point where successive scenes blur or fuse,
in various respects at various rates. One might perform the experiment
with warying luminosity between or within presentations. One might fragment
the successive projectings so that fit is diachronic and like a jigsaw
puzzle. The subject might be acquainted with the aim of the experiment and
what to look for or at least not fail to note. One might vary the rate of
presentation in a gliding way, heterometrically. Etc,

There is an analogy to the Wiener method for using white noise to retrieve
eross-correlation kernels, or randomess to show form, what is in one way a
perfect sampling. My method should in fact break reality or the process of
perception in half so as to show the edges or its important structure, which
is a structure by transformation or intertransformation. The dimensions of
the world and perception should appear in native contrast for the first time.
The point of the randomization of succession is to eliminate interference in
seeing any such structure through the ends of analysis, as simply predictable,
appearing instead. This method should help in seeing the minima and real
terms of perception. The very order inherent in pictures would be used to
offset the routes in between this different order, or the roots of this pigr acre
The very fast and highly complex subliminal processes that ordinarily ,pereeption,
which are otherwise irretrievable, would be divulged. Something of a sense
of scale would be provided for each of these. Further and supremely, the
universal uninanial or n=nomial manifold out of which all possible variety and
complexity of perceptions come, and wherein lies the true diversity (economic
and lavish) of the external world, would be manifest in an almost tangible
fashion. Conceivably a tremendous, lasting, and irreplaceable insight into
all of perception and conception would be had, by the mere experience or by
its early incidence in life or continuance over the lifetims; ie we would learn
to see the structure of things, their relativity and generality; arguments could
be made that all children should be "schooled" with the aid of this autonooscopic
method, Ite scientific exploration could constitute, one of the most important
experiments ever done in psychology, and the method and its results could
reorient and underly all subsequent research within psychology. The method is
therefore analogous to the untapped ability to learn to estimate, value, perceive,
think and act in terms of relative values and patterns of probability.

For sound, it might profit to listen to 2, 3, 20, or a maximal number of
simultaneous or perhaps simltaneously varying pieces of mesic or conversations,
or to alternate and randomly alternate these in time by a complex splicing,
where again the dimensions of things would be divulged.

It is conceivable that all this might lead to a theory of environment or a

new concept of figure and ground. Human thought might become freer, and a new
entertainment and art form found.
